lesson.menu_desc: How a flight is planned, checked and cleared -- and the English that describes a procedure instead of a person -- 37 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 2 -- Inside the Cockpit
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Gabriel Fernandes | Lesson 2 -- Inside the Cockpit
phases: The Words of the Flight Deck

listenings.text: People think the flying starts when the engines start. It does not. By the time I sit down, the route has already been filed, the fuel has been calculated twice, and an alternate airport has been chosen for me by somebody I have never met. My job in that first half hour is to check work that was done by other people. The checklist is read out loud, item by item, even on the four hundredth flight, and it is read out loud precisely because it is the four hundredth. Nothing on that list is difficult. Everything on it has been forgotten by somebody, once, and that is why it is written down.

The question I get asked most is what happens when the weather closes an airport. The honest answer is that almost nothing is decided in that moment, because almost everything was decided before the aircraft left. An alternate had been named in the flight plan hours earlier. The fuel reserve had been loaded for exactly this. So the flight is diverted, the passengers are told, and it looks like a fast decision from the cabin. It is not. It is a slow decision that was made on paper, and then executed quickly.

extra_audio.text: The route is filed with air traffic control the night before. The fuel is calculated from the distance, the weather and the weight. The crew is briefed an hour before departure. The checklist is read out loud before the aircraft is moved. Only then is the aircraft cleared for takeoff.

reading.rtitle: Nothing on That List Is Difficult
paras: A commercial flight is planned long before anybody walks onto the aircraft. The route is chosen from the weather, the winds and the traffic, and it is filed with air traffic control hours ahead. The fuel is calculated from the distance, the forecast and the weight of everything on board, and then it is calculated a second time by a different person. An alternate airport is named in the same document, in case the first one closes.

None of this is done by the pilot. By the time the crew is briefed, most of the decisions have already been made, written down and signed by people the passengers will never see. What the crew does in the first half hour is check work that was done by somebody else.

Then the checklist is read out loud, item by item, on every single flight. Not silently, and not from memory. The reason is not that the items are hard. The reason is that every item on that list was forgotten by somebody, once, and the list is what was written afterwards. Only when the checklist is complete is the aircraft taxied to the runway, and only when the runway is clear is the flight cleared for takeoff.

This is why so much of aviation English is written in the passive. It is not a style choice and it is not politeness. When a procedure matters more than the person carrying it out, English moves the procedure to the front of the sentence and leaves the person out. The fuel was checked. The route was filed. The flight was diverted. Somebody did each of those things, and in that sentence it does not matter who.
reading.source: Written for this lesson from published airline operating procedure.
